paras: The exclusion of Wallace circus's Black workers from Linton, Indiana, took place on July 13, 1903, when residents of the coal-mining town barred the circus's Black employees from entering. The circus left its Black workers, about sixty by one account, outside Linton and gave its show without them, and no violence was reported. The threat followed by a week the expulsion of Black waiters from the town, and the governor held a militia company ready. Southern papers later used the story to answer Northern criticism of the South's treatment of Black people.

By 1903 Linton did not allow Black people to live in the town, according to Indiana dispatches. The Indianapolis Journal traced the rule to Black miners imported from Kentucky by a coal company, "who were afterward driven away," and the New York Sun blamed the coal miners and their families, dating their "prejudice" to a strike. A Kentucky weekly instead dated the expulsion to 1896, and the Columbia State blamed the killing of a white man by a Black man a year earlier.
On July 6, 1903, a crowd estimated at two thousand had forced the Terre Haute caterer Alec Sandison to send his Black waiters out of Linton during an Elks banquet.

The circus, which employed many Black workers, was billed for Linton on Monday, July 13. An Indianapolis dispatch said the people of Linton had given notice days before that the Black employees "must not enter the place." The Savannah Morning News added that a delegation of citizens met the circus twenty miles out and told its managers to leave the Black workers outside. On July 12 Governor Durbin telephoned Sandison about conditions in Linton, and the next morning he called the sheriff and suggested swearing in a large force of deputies. The sheriff conceded that feeling was strong and promised to keep the peace, and the governor quietly held the Terre Haute militia company ready all day.

The circus did not bring its Black workers into Linton, though the accounts place them differently. The Sun placed them at Switz City, twenty miles away; the Indianapolis Journal said sixty were left at the previous stop and, in its Linton report, sent on to Effingham, Illinois; the Columbia State put 65 at a town six miles south. The show played that afternoon to what the Linton correspondent called "a tremendous crowd," and nearly all the mines closed for the day.

According to the Columbia State, a crowd met the circus train and several hundred men inspected it for Black workers. That night, the same account said, special coaches carried the workers through Linton while they "crouched behind the seats to avoid danger."
No arrests or official censure appear in the coverage, which treated the day as trouble avoided.

Indiana papers covered the circus visit as a race riot anticipated and averted, printing it alongside news of the rioting at Evansville. The Indianapolis Journal headed its July 13 report "Riot Feared at Linton" and its next-day report "No Trouble at Linton," and the Louisville Courier-Journal carried a parallel Terre Haute special, "Prospect for Trouble." The New York Sun headed its dispatch "Negroes Barred from Town" and said the circus's precaution "saved trouble," and a Vermont weekly reduced it to a digest line on Linton excluding "negroes belonging to circus company."

Southern papers turned the episode against Northern critics of the South, and Georgia and South Carolina weeklies reprinted it through late July. The Savannah Morning News, in an editorial that mocked Linton's dislike of "the brother in black," concluded: "And yet the North reads the South lectures on its hostility to the colored man!" The Columbia State's account ran in South Carolina weeklies as "Beats the Jim Crow" and "Negroes Not Wanted," ending with the question whether such travel in a Northern state was not "a little worse than the Jim Crow cars down south."
Every account found came from white papers, and none carried a statement from the excluded workers.

The Savannah Morning News said the circus "had to skip the town," but the Linton correspondent of the Indianapolis Journal, writing from the town on the day of the show, reported that it was given to a large crowd; the local report is the better evidence.

reader.title: Exclusion of Wallace circus's Black workers from Linton, Indiana
bases: Linton residents barred the circus's Black workers from entering the town under threat, enforcing a standing rule that no Black person could stay there (A3, A6, A8, A11); no one was attacked.

Independent Indianapolis, Linton and Columbia State accounts agree that the circus's Black workers were kept out of Linton on July 13 under threat (A6, A7, A8, A11); the Savannah editorial agrees on the exclusion but says the show did not play (A9).
